title: A Physics-based and Geometry-aware Reduced-order Framework for Accelerated Part-Scale Thermomechanical Simulation of Additive Friction Stir Deposition Process
abstract: Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) is attractive for naval and aerospace sustainment because it enables high rate, solid state near net shape fabrication and repair of large metallic components. However, full part scale thermomechanical simulations remain computationally demanding because of the moving heat source, progressive material deposition, and evolving geometry. This work presents a physics-based and geometry-aware reduced order framework for rapid prediction of temperature and residual stress fields in part scale AFSD builds. The transient temperature field is represented using a tensor product quadratic B spline basis on a fixed Cartesian background grid, while arbitrary part geometries are embedded using a signed distance function (SDF) and a smooth material indicator. Residual stresses are recovered through an inherent strain formulation in which an offline thermo elasto plastic representative volume element (RVE) simulation supplies a calibrated eigenstrain field that is spatially scaled using the part scale peak temperature history. The thermal formulation is evaluated against published numerical and experimental AFSD data and two sample multilayer builds are simulated as demonstrations. For a four layer thin-wall build, the thermal solution requires approximately 22 s compared to 806 s for the finite element model, while the complete thermo-mechanical framework requires approximately 86.4 s compared to 2,406 s. For a larger 20 layer hollow cylindrical build, the reduced order thermal simulations requires 0.148 to 0.152 h compared with 1.8 h for the finite element model, corresponding to thermal speed-ups of approximately 11.8 to 12.2 times. The complete thermomechanical framework requires 0.346 h compared to 5.4 h for the full finite element analysis, providing an overall speed-up of approximately 15.6 times.

title: Physics-Transfer Learning: A Physics-Constrained Theory for Zero-Shot Generalization Along the Ladder of Complexity
abstract: Reliable out-of-distribution generalization remains a central challenge in machine learning, particularly when models are deployed in data-scarce high-fidelity domains. Existing approaches often rely on statistical distribution alignment, or invariance assumptions that can fail when domain shifts reflect changes in underlying mechanisms. Inspired by a longstanding paradigm in physics that understands complex systems by starting from tractable idealizations and progressively incorporating additional mechanisms and levels of fidelity, we propose physics-transfer (PT) learning, a physics-constrained learning theory for zero-shot generalization along a ladder of complexity. PT constructs chains of anchor domains (CADs) that connect low-cost source domains to complex targets and introduces computable feasibility and reliability indicators for assessing transfer before target-domain labels are observed. Under physical-consistency and stable-representation assumptions, we derive an operational upper bound on target risk in terms of source empirical risk, the PT indicators, and finite-sample errors, and establish convergence as adjacent complexity gaps shrink and data coverage improves. We evaluate PT on excited-state energy prediction in quantum systems and dynamical-transition prediction in classical systems using neural networks trained without target-domain labels. Across substantial distribution shifts, PT yields accurate high-fidelity predictions, while the indicators identify incorrect physical mappings before target-domain prediction fails. These results provide a model-agnostic framework for designing, diagnosing, and controlling generalization in data-scarce learning problems.

title: Regime-Aware Coupled Orchestration of Neural Operator Specialists for Multiphysics Dynamics
abstract: Real-world physics often unfolds over a variety of characteristic lengths and time scales. These non-uniformities are among the main reasons numerical simulations remain expensive when used predictively on practical systems: the same computational domain can contain smooth transport, vortical structures, thin interfaces, reaction fronts, and rapidly relaxing regions. Neural operators are attractive surrogates for such problems. However, a single architecture is still expected to represent all these local behaviours with a single set of weights and a single inductive bias. In this work, we introduce the regime-aware coupled neural orchestrator (RCNO), a framework that learns to distribute and connect a library of local operator specialists in space and time. For every patch, an orchestrator builds a causal query from the current fields, neighbouring halo values, local regime features, patch identity, activity level, and case parameters. The nine expert embeddings exchange two rounds of query-conditioned message passing before an edge-biased cross-attention stage produces a dispatch distribution that can be evaluated sparsely. Local predictions are assembled into a global field and projected onto system-specific physical constraints. A seam-aware extension additionally learns residual corrections across internal patch interfaces. We apply the same orchestration architecture to two qualitatively different systems: reacting flow and Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes (CHNS) dynamics. The results show that useful operator specialisation exists across local regimes, that the advantage of conditional composition increases as the spatial decomposition becomes finer, and, on reacting flow, that explicitly treating patch interfaces improves continuity, PDE consistency, and rollout accuracy.

title: Development of a Particle Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook Method for Rarefied Monatomic Gas Mixtures
abstract: The Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method has long served as a reliable numerical approach for simulating rarefied and non-equilibrium gas flows. Its computational cost, however, increases rapidly as the flow approaches the near-continuum regime. This limitation has motivated the development of kinetic model equations that replace binary collisions with simplified relaxation processes. This paper presents a particle multi-relaxation unified BGK (UBGK) model for monatomic gas mixtures. The model retains pairwise species relaxation and determines the target velocity, temperature, shear stress, and heat flux by matching the corresponding production terms to those of the Boltzmann equation. A stochastic particle algorithm is developed. The model is implemented in SPARTA, and two validation problems are considered: homogeneous relaxation and a Mach 3 flow over a cylinder. In both cases, the UBGK solution reproduces the DSMC reference behavior, including species-dependent relaxation and non-equilibrium shock structure.

title: Advanced computational methods for simulating the classical hydrogen atom in stochastic electrodynamics
abstract: Stochastic electrodynamics (SED) is a theory of nature that seeks to derive key aspects of quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics from a purely classical physics perspective. While SED has been successful in many areas, it has largely failed to stably simulate the 3D classical hydrogen atom. The computational methodology presented here overcomes these foundational challenges. We develop a pseudo-wave formulation that integrates the solid angle in k-space utilizing symmetry, resulting in a significantly reduced memory footprint and lower computational overhead for generating the zero-point radiation spectrum. This optimization is paired with a logarithmic frequency grid, a sliding window tracking the instantaneous Keplerian frequency, and a Tukey smoothing function to eliminate discrete force discontinuities. Integrated via an adaptive RKF45 solver across highly dense grids of up to 100-million bins, these techniques demonstrate the asymptotic convergence of ensemble stability. We show that increasing the grid resolution in the high-frequency domain systematically mitigates artificial electron decay, yielding a simulated probability density function that closely aligns with the quantum mechanical ground state P(r).

title: An Adaptive-Horizon Graph Neural Operator for coupled surrogate morphodynamic modelling
abstract: Morphodynamic simulations require repeated coupling between hydrodynamic solvers, sediment transport modules, and bed updating. For long duration, multi-scenario simulations on large unstructured meshes, such coupling is computationally demanding. This study proposes an Adaptive-Horizon Graph Neural Operator (AH-GNO) that formulates bed evolution as a graph operator learning problem from recent hydrodynamic and topographic states to predict future bed elevation increments. The model operates directly on the native unstructured meshes. The approach integrates area-weighted graph learning, historical state selection, and forecast horizon estimation, allowing the effective history length (K) and update interval (B) to vary with the evolving flow and bed state. Using Telemac2D/GAIA solutions as supervised numerical references, the framework is evaluated on the official Bump and Yen bend benchmarks and on a field-scale application (Waiho River, New Zealand). Results show that the AH-GNO reproduces the main patterns of bedform migration, bend-scale erosion and deposition, and localized bed adjustment. Across the three cases, the tested CPU-GPU deployment reduced post-training bed-update workflow time from 12~1204 s with GAIA to 0.08~3.34 s with AH-GNO. This improvement corresponds to deployment-specific accelerations of approximately 150~360 times relative to 4-core GAIA CPU configurations, and with 105~186 times gains for 20-core CPU configurations. These results suggest that, while retaining hydrodynamic feedback from TELEMAC-2D, a learned operator for bed updating can provide an efficient acceleration component for morphodynamic scenario analysis and rapid coupled simulation.

title: Learnable Splines for Unstructured Neural Operators
abstract: Neural operators approximate solution operators of partial differential equations at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers. Efficient grid-based architectures such as the Fourier neural operator (FNO) assume uniform rectangular grids, whereas engineering simulations use large, irregular, and locally refined meshes. We introduce L-SplineFNO, a memory-efficient neural operator that couples an FNO backbone with a sparse, learnable tensor-product B-spline transfer between unstructured meshes and a latent Cartesian grid. A local normalised scatter avoids the geometry-dependent solve of analytic spline transformation while preserving compact support, partition of unity, and spline smoothness by construction. The neural operator, conditioned on global design and operating parameters, learns the mapping of geometry to the field solution. Across six three-dimensional engineering benchmarks, L-SplineFNO achieves strong predictive accuracy while requiring substantially less memory and compute than baseline operators, scaling to 26.6 million nodes in training and 46 million in inference on a single A100 GPU. It also supports zero-shot super-resolution and efficient closed-form spatial derivatives. Uniquely, the analytic spline decoder yields rigorous prediction bounds over continuous space and uncertain parameters, via Bernstein convex hulls and Taylor models, demonstrated on a 29.2-million-node MAST-U tokamak model.

title: Time-Domain Data-Driven Loewner Reduced-Order Models for Electromagnetic Simulation
abstract: This paper presents a data-driven Loewner framework for constructing reduced-order models (ROMs) from time-domain electromagnetic (EM) simulation data. High-fidelity simulation of microwave devices can be computationally expensive, particularly when fine spatial discretization and long observation windows are required. The proposed method uses transient input-output data to construct Loewner and shifted Loewner matrices, from which a reduced descriptor realization is obtained through singular value decomposition (SVD). The resulting models are identified from a limited training window and used to predict responses over substantially longer time intervals, with prediction windows up to 50 times the duration of the training window. The method is formalized as an explicit, reproducible algorithm and validated against full-order simulations for four microwave structures: a substrate-integrated-waveguide filter, a frequency-selective surface, an evanescent-mode coaxial comb-line filter, and a diplexer. The results demonstrate the potential of Loewner-based identification to provide compact models of electromagnetic responses while reducing the need for repeated full-order simulation.

title: Managing complexity for integrated fusion reactor design using a differentiable graph-based MDAO framework: PROCESS as a case study
abstract: Integrated design of nuclear fusion reactors requires combining an increasingly large number of models from different disciplines self-consistently, with model selection and parametrisation changing between design studies. Manual definition of execution order and solvers for cyclic dependencies is error-prone, inefficient, and inflexible. We propose to use a generic graph-based coordination and execution core that enables automated execution order, cycle detection, and solver architecture specification for any set of models or parametrisation. To this end, a computational dependency graph of purely functional models is extended by a conditional node and nesting edges, treating solvers and optimisers in the same way. A minimal set of graph operations then allows for fine-tuned control on feedback resolution, making both optimiser and solver architectures easily reconfigurable. Existing monolithic multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation (MDAO) architectures can be recovered by sequentially applying these operations. The cottax package implements this extended dependency graph, graph operations, executability checks, and a JAX-based execution layer. This execution layer eliminates runtime overhead and provides native gradient computation through the whole graph. As a proof of principle, cottax is then applied to the PROCESS systems code. Graph sequencing shows that for PROCESS only three small coupled components need to be solved every optimiser iteration. Monolithic MDAO architectures are then assigned to seven different PROCESS configurations, demonstrating the ease of (re)configuring its architecture. Compared to PROCESS, the sequencing and execution back-end together yield a two to three orders of magnitude reduction in model runtime during optimisation. cottax is currently being considered as the basis for developing an integrated stellarator MDAO framework.

title: Azimuthal Instability in Oscillating Liquid Jets by the Weber Number Variations
abstract: This paper investigates the dependence of azimuthal mode growth rate of oscillating liquid laminar jets on the Weber number. The oscillating liquid laminar jets were simulated over a range of Weber numbers. The simulation setup was validated by comparing the instantaneous interface shapes and the visible azimuthal mode from experimental measurements. As the Weber number increases, the spreading angle rises due to the small surface tension, and higher azimuthal modes are observed. Fourier Transform analysis is used to find the exact azimuthal mode of the simulation results. The dominant azimuthal mode increases as the Weber number increases. A power-law dependence of the growth rate on the Weber number is identified, with the obtained exponents showing good agreement with linear instability analysis. Furthermore, the rescaled Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) results collapse onto a single growth curve for each azimuthal mode, validating the proposed power-law for predicting the growth rates of oscillating liquid jets.

title: PINN-LPCDD: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition for Compressible Multi-Medium Flows
abstract: The physics-informed neural network (PINN) faces significant challenges when solving compressible multi-medium flows, including the inability to locate interface positions, poor approximation of discontinuities, and difficulty in handling high-pressure-ratio problems between media with large stiffness differences. To address these issues, we propose PINN with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition (PINN-LPCDD), a framework that incorporates the sharp interface method (SIM) into PINNs for solving compressible multi-medium flows. Firstly, we design separate sub-networks for each medium with learnable parameters to automatically learn interface positions, so that the domain decomposition is physically consistent, and the contact discontinuity at the interface is naturally sharp. Secondly, the Euler equations with artificial viscosity are solved to enhance robustness when handling problems involving shock waves. Lastly, the scaling invariance of the Euler equations is exploited to facilitate the solution of high pressure ratio problems. Numerical experiments on air-air, air-helium, air-water, and air-R22 problems demonstrate the acceptable accuracy of the proposed method in simulating multi-medium flows.

title: Simulation of centrifugal separation of particles with equal sedimentation velocities
abstract: Conventional centrifugal sedimentation cannot readily separate particles with the same sedimentation velocities. Density gradient centrifugation, although highly selective, exposes delicate particles such as drug delivery system (DDS) nanoparticles and exosomes to high osmotic pressure that can cause shrinkage, rupture, or expansion. To separate particles with equal or similar sedimentation velocities while preserving their properties, we propose two methods that exploit thermal fluctuations (Brownian motion): the centrifugal Brownian ratchet method, which uses asymmetric structures, and the centrifugal wavy-channel method, which uses geometric barriers. Two-dimensional Brownian dynamics simulations combining Stokes-Einstein diffusion with centrifugal sedimentation were performed, and particle transport was analyzed using the P\'eclet number. In the ratchet method, particles with identical sedimentation velocities but different P\'eclet numbers showed statistically distinct mean arrival positions and times. In the wavy-channel method, periodic entropic barriers interacting with differences in transport properties produced arrival-time differences, achieving temporal separation even for particles with identical sedimentation velocities or P\'eclet numbers. Both methods separate particles without relying on sedimentation-velocity differences and are expected to preserve particle properties. Because they neither depend on electrical properties nor require a change of medium, they may also be applicable to particles in liquid metals, oils, organic solvents, and ionic liquids.

title: Foundation-Model Supervision of Distilled Potentials for Million-Atom Molecular Dynamics
abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials distilled from foundation models enable fast large-scale molecular dynamics (MD), but they can fail locally in chemical environments that their training data did not sample. System-averaged error metrics and small random audits often miss such sparse or isolated failures. Here we use an exact equivariant foundation model, MACE-MPA-0, to check every atom of million-atom production simulations. Reorganizing two-layer MACE inference into a receiver-chunked three-pass schedule that keeps no per-edge intermediates resident reduces the marginal memory per atom 340-fold, evaluates up to $2.86\times10^{7}$ atoms on a single H200 GPU, and supervises $10^{6}$-atom trajectories in LAMMPS at 1.3% of the run time. Distilled MACE students run four to nine times slower than NEP89 with 0.95-1.28 times the teacher's force error against density functional theory (DFT). In molten SiO$_2$, whole-system checks uncover a persistent tail of under-coordinated atoms hidden by the system-averaged error and an isolated, unphysical O-O contact that a 1% random audit misses 94% of the time. On-the-fly retraining on teacher-labelled 13-{\AA} clusters, with the force loss restricted to their inner 6 {\AA}, removes three quarters of the failure tail and the kilobar-level pressure biases in SiO$_2$ and compressed water; the repair converges to the teacher, not to DFT.

title: Plastic Flow Rule Based on Dislocation Link Velocity
abstract: We develop a theory for the plastic shear rate $\dot{\gamma}_i$ on each slip system $i$ of face-centered cubic (FCC) single crystals, by integrating the shear rate contributions $\dot{\gamma}_i(l)$ from dislocation links of length $l$. A generalized Orowan equation expresses $\dot{\gamma}_i(l)$ in terms of the link density $n_i(l)$ and the average link velocity $v_i(l)$. This model accurately reproduces the discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) shear-rate data for all 12 slip systems across 99 loading orientations. In particular, it explains why the plastic shear rate depends exponentially on the resolved shear stress $\tau_i$, as reported previously, in the absence of any thermally activated mechanism. This dependence arises from the exponential tail of $n_i(l)$ filtered through the threshold-like velocity function $v_i(l)$. Furthermore, $v_i(l)$ is well approximated by a single two-dimensional function $v(\tau_i,l)$ for all these slip systems. The link velocity is therefore governed mainly by $\tau_i$ and $l$, with only a minor effect from the complex interactions between slip systems. These interactions instead manifest themselves mainly through $n_i(l)$. As a demonstration of the effect of the link-length distribution on the slip rate, we show that even when $\tau_i$ is limited to a narrow window, the shear rates still span two orders of magnitude. The supply of long links is therefore the dominant factor controlling slip-system activity, outweighing the direct effect of $\tau_i$ on the link velocity.

title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency
abstract: Developing a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is accurate for the specific conditions under which it will be applied, rather than simply for the predefined configurations chosen by the model developer, is a significant challenge in atomistic simulation. Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by closing the loop between candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating. Here, we survey more than seventy studies, with an emphasis on work from 2020 to 2026, to understand how active learning has evolved from a niche, on-the-fly training technique for query-by-committee and Gaussian process force fields into a diverse family of data-efficient strategies. he reviewed examples include on-the-fly molecular dynamics, active data selection for fine-tuning pretrained models, kernel- and representation-based acquisition using frozen pretrained models, and reaction-aware sampling for chemical systems far from equilibrium. We explore the use of active learning in elemental and alloy mechanics, hydrogen and ion diffusion, ferroelectrics and effective Hamiltonians of functional materials, reactive and photochemical dynamics, high-entropy and compositionally disordered materials, as well as generative and autonomous material discovery pipelines. Drawing on a growing body of critical, methodologically self-aware literature, we also show that this achievement carries systematic caveats. Uncertainty estimates are not interchangeable across model architectures and are frequently the least reliable exactly where they matter most. We close by discussing the outlook for standardized, uncertainty-calibrated, and observable-targeted active-learning workflows in the foundation-model era.
